subject: Pathology
summary: Nitric oxide (NO) is a gaseous signaling molecule produced by endothelial cells and macrophages. It regulates vascular tone, immune responses, and smooth‑muscle relaxation. In disease, NO imbalance contributes to inflammation, thrombosis, and organ dysfunction.

sections.p: NO is synthesized from L‑arginine by nitric‑oxide synthase (NOS). Its production is measured indirectly by plasma nitrite/nitrate or urinary excretion, and by nasal NO in primary ciliary dyskinesia.
b: NO is a short‑lived free radical, not stored in the body.

t.b: Assesses systemic NO production; low levels suggest endothelial dysfunction; high levels may indicate excessive inflammatory NO.
Low values are diagnostic of primary ciliary dyskinesia; normal values rule it out.

sections.p: NO imbalance is graded by clinical context: mild endothelial dysfunction (e.g., hypertension), moderate inflammatory overproduction (sepsis), severe depletion (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria).
b: Severity correlates with organ involvement and laboratory markers such as lactate dehydrogenase or D‑dimer.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by source: endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory cytokines, hemolysis, and genetic defects.
b: Endothelial dysfunction: hypertension, diabetes, smoking.
Inflammatory overproduction: sepsis, autoimmune disease, malaria.
Hemolysis: PNH, sickle cell crisis.
Genetic: primary ciliary dyskinesia (low nasal NO).

sections.p: Clinical features depend on the underlying cause: hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, hemolytic anemia, or chronic cough with nasal congestion.
b: Hypertension with normal renal function.
Pulmonary hypertension with dyspnea and clubbing.
Hemolytic anemia with jaundice and dark urine.
Chronic sinusitis with low nasal NO.

sections.p: Investigations focus on identifying the source of NO imbalance and organ damage.

t.b: Identifies autoimmune hemolysis; positive test indicates immune-mediated NO consumption.
Elevated in thrombotic states like PNH; indicates NO‑mediated platelet activation.
Assesses pulmonary hypertension; high pulmonary pressures suggest NO deficiency.
High levels in hemolysis; correlates with NO scavenging.

sections.p: Complications arise when NO depletion or excess leads to organ failure.
b: Thrombosis (hepatic vein, pulmonary).
Acute respiratory distress syndrome.
Severe anemia leading to hypoxia.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support organ function, and modulate NO pathways.
b: In PNH: complement inhibition to reduce hemolysis and NO loss.
In sepsis: early antibiotics and source control to curb inflammatory NO.
In hypertension: ACE inhibitors or ARBs to restore NO production.
In pulmonary hypertension: endothelin receptor antagonists and phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors to enhance NO signaling.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of hemolysis markers, blood pressure, and pulmonary pressures is essential.
b: Annual CBC and LDH in PNH.
Blood pressure checks in hypertension.
Pulmonary function tests in chronic lung disease.
Asthma (chronic cough).
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (dyspnea).
Rheumatic heart disease (pulmonary hypertension).

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite NO imbalance.
b: Normal nitrite in early endothelial dysfunction; need functional flow tests.
Low nasal NO can be seen in allergic rhinitis; confirm with ciliary function tests.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hemolysis with sudden drop in hemoglobin
Sudden onset of chest pain with evidence of thrombosis

faq.q: What is the main source of NO in blood vessels?
faq.a: Endothelial cells via endothelial nitric‑oxide synthase (eNOS).

faq.q: Why is NO important in sepsis?
faq.a: It mediates vasodilation and microcirculatory perfusion; excess production can cause hypotension.

faq.q: Can NO levels be measured directly?
faq.a: NO is too short‑lived; we measure stable metabolites like nitrite/nitrate or use indirect tests such as nasal NO.

exam: Explain how NO deficiency contributes to pulmonary hypertension in primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Describe the laboratory work‑up for a patient with suspected paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
Outline the therapeutic approach to NO overproduction in septic shock.
